notes:
Docket told a university its brand name was inconsistent. Every page on the site spelled it the same way.

When Docket reads your titles, it has to work out which side of the separator holds your company name. "Shop | Acme Roofing" puts it last; "Stripe | Payments" puts it first. Both conventions are common, and picking the wrong one turns every page name on the site into an alternative spelling of your company.

The first thing Docket consults is your domain: whichever side of the title looks like your hostname is the brand side. That is usually decisive, and it was written that way for good reason.

It was counting the wrong thing. It counted how many *distinct* fragments on each side resembled the domain, rather than how many *titles*. A site whose every page ends with the same brand contributes exactly one distinct fragment, however many pages it has — while each page name that happens to mention the brand contributes another.

On a university we audited, every one of the forty titles read "<Page name> | RIT". That is about as consistent as a title convention gets. But five distinct page names mention the university — "History of RIT", "Research at RIT", "RIT Life", "Faces of RIT", "Giving to RIT" — so the score came out five against one, the page-name side won, and Docket decided the company was called "Contact", "Disclaimer", "Athletics", "Cookie Settings", and thirty-six other things. It then reported that the brand appears two different ways and quoted two page names back to the owner as evidence.

Counted by titles instead of by distinct spellings, the same site reads twenty against five: the suffix is on every page, the mentions are on five of them. Docket now reads the brand as "RIT", and the finding correctly does not fire.

Brand-first sites are unaffected. When the brand is the side that repeats — "Stripe | Payments", "Stripe | Billing" — it still wins, which is the case this logic was originally written to protect, and the one a naive "always take the suffix" rule breaks.

**Also in this release:** two internal notes recording what a page render actually costs, and one recording a measurement we withdrew after finding the run-to-run variation was larger than the effect we had reported.
